L-15; Limited Partnership Regulation, Alta. Reg. 264/1997; FINTRAC Regulations under the PCMLTFA; Alberta Corporate Registry beneficial ownership information requirements.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certified notarized copy of valid passport for each general partner and each individual owning 25% or more of the limited partnership
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary public or commissioner for oaths in the partner's country of residence
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille if the country of origin is a party; otherwise consular legalization at a Canadian diplomatic mission

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Standing or equivalent certificate of legal existence for each corporate general partner
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Home-country companies registry or equivalent competent authority

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Incumbency and register of directors and officers for each corporate general partner
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Corporate secretary or registered agent of the corporate general partner

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory PEP, OFAC, UN, and domestic sanctions screening is required for all general partners, limited partners holding at or above the 25% UBO threshold, and authorized signatories. Screening must be performed at the outset and periodically at least annually against FINTRAC guidance and Canadian sanctions under the Special Economic Measures Act and United Nations Act, the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List, the Consolidated United Nations Security Council Sanctions List, and reputable international risk databases. A positive PEP or sanctions hit requires senior management approval, enhanced due diligence, and where warranted a suspicious transaction report to FINTRAC.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry - online name search and corporate access service provided by the Government of Alberta (alberta.ca/corporate-registry)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Statutory corporate names must be in English and/or French using Latin-script characters. Foreign script names or non-English transliterations are generally not acceptable unless rendered in English or French. The proposed name must be distinguishable, not misleading, and must contain the appropriate legal element such as 'Limited' or 'L.P.' in accordance with Alberta corporate registry rules.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the NUANS name search report is rejected or the proposed name is refused by Alberta Corporate Registry, the applicant must file a written administrative review request within 30 days of the rejection notice, addressed to the Registrar of Alberta Corporate Registry, stating the grounds and proposing corrected name alternatives. A name search report is valid for 90 days and cannot be extended; a new report is required after expiry. If the Registrar maintains the refusal, the applicant may commence judicial review in the Court of King's Bench of Alberta under the Administrative Procedures and Jurisdiction Act, RSA 2000, c. A-3, supported by affidavit evidence and applicable court filing fees.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office arrangement is permissible for an Alberta limited partnership only if the provider supplies a physical street address in Alberta capable of receiving service of process and maintaining statutory records. A post-office box or a mail-forwarding-only arrangement is not sufficient. For a low-risk mobile utility application company using an app-store freemium model, a virtual office through a licensed registered agent or law firm is acceptable for the registered office obligation, provided the partnership maintains adequate records and commercial substance documentation to support its pass-through tax treatment.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low. Estimated annual probability of an unannounced physical on-site inspection is approximately 5% for an Alberta limited partnership in the ISIC 6201 software sector with no tax, AML, or sanctions red flags. Compliance with registered office, records-keeping, and FINTRAC obligations materially reduces inspection risk.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Partnership Act, RSA 2000, c P-3, Part 2 (Limited Partnerships), ss. 51–79, including s. 51 (registration), s. 53 (contents of registration) and s. 66 (effect of registration).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta (filings accepted online via Corporate Registry's authorized registry service provider system at corporate-registry.alberta.ca).
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Application for Registration of a Limited Partnership (Form LP-1) and supporting Declaration, resulting in issuance of a Certificate of Registration.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital for Alberta limited partnerships. Contributions are fixed by the Limited Partnership Agreement and may be cash, property, or promissory notes; no escrow account is mandated for capital contributions. Form LP-1 must declare the contributions made or to be made by each limited partner. At least one general partner must be resident in Canada.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLUTIONS OF THE GENERAL PARTNER OF [INSERT] LIMITED PARTNERSHIP, ADOPTED BY UNANIMOUS WRITTEN RESOLUTION IN LIEU OF A MEETING ON [DATE]: (1) SUBSCRIPTION: The General Partner approves the execution of the Limited Partnership Agreement, the admission of the founding Limited Partners, and the subscription of initial partnership interests, the aggregate capital contribution being recorded in the Partnership's books. (2) REGISTERED OFFICE: The registered office and records address of the Partnership in Alberta is fixed at [ADDRESS], Alberta. (3) OFFICERS: [NAME] is appointed as the General Partner's authorized representative to complete filings with Alberta Corporate Registry and the Canada Revenue Agency, including Business Number, GST/HST and partnership information return (T5013) registrations. (4) EFFECTIVE DATE: These resolutions take effect immediately upon registration of the Partnership. APPROVED AND CONFIRMED.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry via an authorized NUANS search house or registry agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a NUANS corporate name search request for the proposed legal name, which must contain 'Limited Partnership', 'L.P.', or 'L.P.' style permissible abbreviation. Ensure the name is distinctive from existing Alberta corporations, extra-provincial entities, limited partnerships, and registered trade-marks. Review the NUANS report for confusing similarity; if clear, retain the certified report for filing with Step 2.
required_dossiers: Proposed legal name and optional alternate names (up to 3)
Declaration of proposed name usage signed by the general partner
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the NUANS report flags a conflicting name, file a written objection or amend the proposed name and perform a fresh NUANS search within 30 days; no registry fee refund is issued on refused names.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registration of the Limited Partnership (Form LP-1) with Alberta Corporate Registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta (online portal or authorized service provider)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete and execute Form LP-1, including: the Partnership's full legal name; the Alberta registered office address (street address, not a post office box); the general partner's full legal name and Canadian residential or corporate registered address; the aggregate contribution of each limited partner and the nature (money, property, or services); and the statement regarding the general partner's Canadian residency. Attach the certified NUANS report, execute the required declaration, and pay the $90 CAD filing fee (approx. $67 USD). Upon approval, the Registry issues a Certificate of Registration, which is conclusive evidence of formation.
required_dossiers: Certified NUANS name search report (issued within prior 90 days)
Consent to act and Canadian residency confirmation of the general partner
Proof of registered office address (lease or landlord consent letter)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registry issues a query or rejection notice, respond in writing within 10 business days with corrected declarations or supporting attestations; resubmit the amended Form LP-1 with any incremental fee, and request expedited re-review if the APLR queue causes delay.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Federal Business Number and Tax Registration with the CRA
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – Business Registration Online (BRO) portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After obtaining the Certificate of Registration, register the Partnership for a federal Business Number (BN). Elect for GST/HST registration (RT program account), including registration for the goods and services tax applicable to taxable Canadian supplies derived from app subscriptions; register for payroll (RP) accounts if employees are engaged. Note that the limited partnership is a pass-through entity: it obtains a BN, files an annual Partnership Information Return (T5013), and allocates income to partners, but does not pay income tax at the partnership level. Ensure the general partner's legal name and the Partnership BN appear on all CRA correspondence.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Registration issued by Alberta Corporate Registry
Executed Limited Partnership Agreement or contribution schedule
General partner's personal identification and authorization matrix
Projected revenue information for GST/HST registration election
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA rejects or queries the registration, file a written correction via CRA's 'Change Business Registration' service or call the Business Window (1-800-959-5525); provide the BN program account reference and supporting declaration, and await confirmed registration notice before invoicing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Municipal Business Licence and Occupational Premises Clearance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Applicable Alberta municipal business licensing authority (e.g., City of Calgary Business Licence Office or City of Edmonton Program Services)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Apply for a general business licence for the software development office, specifying ISIC 6201/NAICS 511210 (software publishers). Submit the lease or occupancy agreement, the Partnership's Certificate of Registration, and the general partner's authorized signatory details. Confirm that the premises zoning permits office use and that the building holds a valid fire safety occupancy permit. For home-based operations, verify the municipality's home occupation regulations and submit the landlord's written consent.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Registration of the Limited Partnership
General partner's identification and municipal fee payment
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the municipality denies or conditions the licence due to zoning or occupancy issues, submit a zoning compliance letter, revised floor plans, or written landlord consent; appeal an adverse decision to the municipality's business licence review committee or development appeal board within 14–30 days as prescribed by the applicable bylaw.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable – ISIC 6201 (software publishing and mobile application development) is not a manufacturing or extractive activity in Alberta and does not require an industrial operating permit from Alberta's industrial licensing agencies.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Alberta Municipal General Business Licence (required for office operations); no provincial industrial operating license or manufacturing permit applies.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt – Digital software publishing is not a listed activity under the Environmental Protection and Enhancement Act, RSA 2000, c E-12, Schedule of Activities; no full EIA report or registration is triggered by mobile application development operations.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: N/A – Office-based development produces no stationary combustion source, process wastewater, or regulated VOC emissions. Compliance obligations are limited to proper disposal of electronic waste through Alberta's designated material management rules and adherence to municipal solid waste diversion bylaws; no provincial effluent or air emission discharge thresholds are triggered.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: The leased office must hold a valid fire safety compliance certificate under the Alberta Fire Code (fire extinguishers, illuminated exits, non-flammable storage, and egress capacity). The General Partner must complete an Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) workplace hazard assessment under the OHS Act, RSA 2000, c O-2 and the OHS Code, covering ergonomic workstations, electrical safety, and first-aid supplies. A municipal occupancy clearance or development permit endorsement confirming the premises are suitable for office use is required before staff commence work.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), under the Minister of National Revenue; CRA Business Portal at https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/cra-business-portal.html; Alberta corporate and partnership income tax is administered by CRA under the Canada–Alberta Tax Collection Agreement; Alberta Registries administers LP registration under the Partnership Act (RSA 2000, c P-3).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: The Alberta Limited Partnership must first be registered with Alberta Registries (or, if formed outside Alberta, registered as an extra-provincial limited partnership). For federal tax identity, the LP applies for a CRA Business Number (BN) through Business Registration Online or, for non-resident partnerships, by filing RC391 (Request for a Business Number and Certain CRA Program Accounts) or by contacting CRA Business Registration. The BN is the statutory tax identification number; the LP must open a BN/GST-HST program account if taxable supplies in Canada exceed the small-supplier threshold. The LP files partnership information returns on Form T5013 when it carries on business in Canada and has Canadian-resident partners or Canadian-source income; non-resident partners may require a Canadian representative for service of process. Alberta does not issue a separate provincial tax ID for a limited partnership; provincial income tax liabilities are settled through CRA-administered returns using the same BN.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Pass_Through_Eligible. An Alberta LP is fiscally transparent under the Income Tax Act: the partnership is not generally a taxpayer; each partner includes its share of partnership income or loss. For GST/HST purposes, however, a partnership is treated as a separate person under subsection 272(1) of the Excise Tax Act and may be a GST/HST registrant in its own capacity. A non-resident LP carrying on business in Canada creates Canadian-source business income for its non-resident partners, subject to Part I tax and information-reporting obligations.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No U.S.-style check-the-box election is available under Canadian law. Entity classification is determined by statutory and common-law legal form. An Alberta LP is a partnership, not an electable corporation. Canada's hybrid-mismatch rules (Income Tax Act sections 18.2 and 18.3) may reduce or deny deductions for payments involving hybrid entities, but they do not provide an affirmative check-the-box election. No other relevant entity classification elections apply to an Alberta LP for federal income tax purposes.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) under Part IX of the Excise Tax Act; Alberta applies only the 5% federal GST because it has no provincial sales tax or HST component.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000: a supplier becomes required to register once taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000 in a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters. Non-resident suppliers of digital services and remote cross-border supplies using the simplified non-resident GST/HST registration framework are subject to the same CAD 30,000 economic threshold.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada has no mandatory real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction control, or government e-stamping regime for GST/HST. Registrants must issue sales invoices or simplified receipts containing prescribed information under section 221 of the Excise Tax Act, and must retain electronic records that support the tax position. Returns and payments are submitted electronically through CRA's GST/HST NETFILE/portal system, but this is not a real-time clearance mechanism. Where Apple IAP or Google Play Billing is used, the app-store payment reports and settlement statements must be retained and reconciled to the LP's books for audit support.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating is available for: (i) tangible personal property exported by the vendor from Canada under Schedule VI, Part V, Division I of the Excise Tax Act, provided documentary evidence of export is obtained; and (ii) services and intangible personal property, including mobile app licences and downloads, supplied to non-resident persons, provided the supply is not in respect of real property situated in Canada and is not for use wholly in Canada. For app-store sales, the vendor must establish non-resident customer status through records such as billing addresses, app-store territory data, IP addresses, and the customer's download account country. Supplies of digital apps to Canadian residents through Apple IAP or Google Play Billing are generally subject to 5% GST unless a statutory zero-rating provision applies. Zero-rating is claimed on the GST/HST return and may give rise to a refund.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canada Customs Export Declaration (Form B13A or CERS electronic export reporting) for physical exports where required by the Customs Act; not applicable to pure digital downloads
Commercial invoice and app-store sales report from Apple IAP or Google Play Billing showing transaction-level sales territory
Bill of lading, air waybill, or other carrier transport document for physical exports
Evidence of export such as customs stamp, export coder, carrier certificate, or logistics release proof
Executed software licence agreement, terms of service, or app-store merchant agreement demonstrating supply is to a non-resident recipient
App-store settlement statement, bank statement, or inward remittance/foreign-currency records evidencing receipt of foreign payment
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA regularly audits export zero-rating claims. Failure to maintain sufficient documentary evidence can result in reassessment of output GST/HST, interest, and penalties, plus retroactive clawback of previously allowed zero-rated refunds. The CRA may reassess within four years of the assessment date, or seven years where misrepresentation, fraud, or neglect is shown. Civil penalties may include the greater of fixed amounts and percentages of understated tax, and gross-negligence or false-statement penalties can reach 50% of the net understatement. Egregious cases may be referred for criminal prosecution under the Excise Tax Act and the Criminal Code.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), constituted under the Bank of Canada Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. B-2), is the central monetary authority. Canada maintains no standalone foreign-exchange control administration; prudential supervision of banks is vested in the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), payment-system governance in Payments Canada, and cross-border anti-money-laundering surveillance in FINTRAC under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA). The Minister of Finance retains residual statutory powers over exchange-rate intervention through the Currency Act and the Exchange Fund Act, although intervention is exceptional. For a mobile utility app business, no sector-specific foreign-investment screening applies under the Investment Canada Act at the limited-partnership scale.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar (CAD) is a fully convertible hard currency. Canada has accepted Article VIII obligations of the IMF Articles of Agreement, prohibiting exchange restrictions on current international transactions and discriminatory currency arrangements; capital-account movements are likewise unrestricted. There is no convertibility licensing, no central-bank approval for capital inflows, no exchange allocation, and no statutory restriction on profit remittance by a non-resident limited partner. Practical hurdles are fiscal and documentary only: a non-resident partner is subject to Canadian Part XIII withholding tax on taxable allocations or distributions (default 25%, reduced under an applicable income tax treaty), and to CRS/FATCA reporting. The Alberta limited partnership must also satisfy bank-level source-of-funds and beneficial-ownership verification when converting foreign-currency inflows into CAD.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no mandatory surrender, repatriation deadline, or compulsory conversion ratio for export proceeds or app-store revenues. An Alberta LP may retain Apple IAP and Google Play Billing proceeds in USD/EUR or any currency and convert to CAD at will. The only statutory obligations are informational: every international electronic funds transfer of CAD 10,000 or more must be reported by the financial intermediary to FINTRAC as an Electronic Funds Transfer Report (EFTR), and any person physically importing or exporting currency or monetary instruments of CAD 10,000 or more must file the Cross-Border Currency or Monetary Instruments Report (CBSA Form E677). No central-bank declaration is required for standard SWIFT business payments below those thresholds.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account (segregated CAD/USD ledger for non-resident LP capital contributions, operated with capital-call matching) and Operational Account (SWIFT-enabled multicurrency CAD, USD, EUR current account with ACSS direct debit and RBC Treasury Management portal)

Capital Escrow Account and Operational Account; TD's U.S. network (TD Bank, N.A.) provides same-bank USD receiving, reducing correspondent friction for non-resident partners funding from the United States

Capital Escrow Account and Operational Account; BMO's digital FX and payments modules (BMO Radicle, BMO Payment Edge) offer lower-cost SWIFT and treasury-liquidity sweeps suitable for a subscription-app treasury
Capital Escrow Account and Operational Account; CIBC is well-provisioned for marketplace and software-payments settlement streams, including Apple and Google payout aggregation
Capital Escrow Account and Operational Account; Scotiabank's global correspondent hubs support partner originations from Latin America and the Caribbean without secondary due-diligence friction
Capital Escrow Account and Operational Account; viable if a Quebec presence is later added, but non-resident-controlled LP onboarding currently takes longer and offers fewer digital treasury features

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility: MEDIUM-HIGH as a secondary clearing engine; LOW as the sole or settlement bank. Canadian law reserves deposit-taking to chartered banks, trust and loan companies, and cooperative-credit associations; an offshore digital EMI (e.g., a UK FCA-authorised or EU-licensed electronic-money institution) cannot legally present itself as a Canadian bank or offer CDIC-insured accounts to the LP. An EMI may, however, register as a Foreign Money Services Business (MSB) via FINTRAC and, under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPA) with its Bank of Canada registration regime becoming effective in 2025, may also require registration as a Retail Payment Service Provider. Practically, a registered EMI (e.g., Wise Platform, Airwallex, or similar) may hold pre-funded balances in an omnibus account at an authorised Canadian bank, execute foreign-currency payouts, and offer tight-margin FX conversion; those balances remain uninsured and rank as unsecured claims in an EMI insolvency. Recommended structure: operate a Tier-1 bank account as the ledger-of-record, use the EMI only for vendor disbursement, mass payouts, and spot FX optimisation, and sweep the EMI ledger back to the Tier-1 account at least monthly. Direct deposit of Apple IAP and Google Play Billing settlements into an EMI must be screened against geographical prohibition lists (e.g., OFAC sanctions), and the EMI must maintain a compliant merchant descriptor to avoid transaction misclassification.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No statutory mandate for physical branch appearance exists, provided the bank follows FINTRAC Remote Identity Verification guidance (e.g., dual-process credit-file verification, notarial certification, or liveness-checked video review of a government-issued passport). In practice, the Tier-1 Canadian banks will not open a corporate account for a non-resident-controlled LP without satisfying at least one of the following: (i) physical in-branch attendance by an authorised signatory at a Canadian (or correspondent) branch with valid photo ID; (ii) a live video interview accompanied by a notarised identity and authority package and a certified copy of the Alberta Corporate Registry Certificate of Status; or (iii) a banker's introduction from the home-country bank of the General Partner under a correspondent correlation. The LP must maintain a registered office address in Alberta (a corporate-services address is accepted), appoint a resident Canadian compliance contact (e.g., tax counsel or a professional fiduciary), and provide the Alberta corporate access number (CAN) at onboarding. End-to-end onboarding: 3-8 weeks for a standard-risk LP; BMO and CIBC digital account-opening portals are materially faster (2-3 weeks).

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident control structure: the corporate General Partner and a majority of limited partners are tax-resident outside Canada, triggering beneficial-ownership opacity and reverse-hybrid abuse red flags.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Current Certificate of Status from the Alberta Corporate Registry; executed limited partnership agreement and first-amendment documents; corporate register extract of the General Partner; a complete UBO schedule identifying all natural persons holding 25% or more of income or capital; CRS self-certification (CRS-1) and FATCA Form W-8BEN-E per partner; tax-residency certificates from each partner's jurisdiction; sworn source-of-wealth and source-of-funds declarations; and the bank's own AML questionnaire signed by the General Partner.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: App-store revenue pattern: high-volume, low-ticket microtransactions flowing through Apple IAP and Google Play Billing, which automated underwriting may interpret as a pass-through or transaction-laundering gateway.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Apple Developer Program and Google Play Console registration certificates; monthly settlement and payout files mapping App Store Connect and Google Play Reporting to expected bank credits; user-country aggregated download data; refund and chargeback monitoring policies; promotional-code audit trails; and a business-plan annex describing the freemium conversion funnel and average revenue per paying user.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Shell-profile concern: no operational premises, a single registered-office address, and no Canadian employees create a nominee-corporation presumption.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Registered-office services agreement or sub-lease inside Alberta; administrative utility bill at the registered address; payroll provider report or consultant agreements of the app-development team; repository access logs (GitHub and Apple Developer account stewardship); a product-dashboard screenshot showing live app-store presence; and engagement letters of Canadian legal and accounting advisors.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Layered pass-through capital: identical-tranche capital contributions from multiple non-resident partners routed through one correspondent, presenting structuring and proceeds-of-crime red flags.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: General Partner resolutions approving the capital call; individually executed capital-call notices stating amount, currency, and bank route; MT103 wire confirmations from each remitting bank; three months of source-funds bank statements per contributing partner; sanctions and adverse-media screening certificates issued within 60 days; and a capital-introduction memorandum prepared by the Canadian law firm that completed the LPA drafting.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Part XIII distribution mechanics: anticipated remittances to non-resident partners may appear as conduit-payment arrangements if the LP does not evidence its withholding obligation.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Signed Part XIII withholding policy (default 25%, treaty-reduced where applicable); T5013 partnership information return confirmation from the tax preparer; CRA NR302 waiver application records where applicable; distribution resolutions with computed gross-up and withholding entries; and an opinion letter by a Canadian tax lawyer confirming that distributions will be computed under section 96 of the Income Tax Act (Canada) and will not be recharacterised as a conduit arrangement.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: All non-resident LP contributions route as SWIFT MT103 wire transfers (or Canadian wire for domestic partners) to the Capital Escrow Account at the Tier-1 bank. Each credit must be pre-registered by a capital-call notice containing: (a) the LP's full legal name, (b) capital-account number, (c) contribution amount and currency, (d) source-country partner name and address, and (e) the payment reference 'CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION - [PARTNER NAME] - [ACCOUNT NUMBER]'. For USD remittances to a Canadian-dollar escrow account, the sponsoring bank typically receives funds at its U.S. correspondent (e.g., BMO Bank N.A. or RBC Bank) and forwards to Canada through SWIFT, converting to CAD at a specified rate. The bank will tag the purpose under the Canadian Balance of Payments classification as 'FDI inflow - equity participation' for Statistics Canada reporting. FINTRAC automatically receives EFTR filings on any single or cumulative 24-hour transaction at or above CAD 10,000. At amounts above CAD 1 million, the bank will require each partner's source-of-funds attestation before crediting and will not accept third-party payments (payments originating from an account not in the partner's own name). Clearing latency: 1-3 business days for USD/EUR/GBP; same-day for CAD-denominated wires originating within Payments Canada.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: The treasury deploys four clearing rails: (1) SWIFT MT103 for all international supplier invoices, intercompany licensing fees, contractor payroll, and non-resident distributions, each MT103 including an electronic beneficiary reference and the appropriate purpose phrase (for distributions: 'DISTRIBUTION PER PARTNERSHIP RESOLUTION [DATE]'); (2) Commercial Letters of Credit (UCP 600) for high-value equipment or outsourcing contracts above C$50,000, issued by the Tier-1 bank and confirmed by a beneficiary-country advising bank; (3) ACSS (Automated Clearing Settlement System) / EFT for all CAD-denominated domestic vendor payments, insurance, and hosting subscriptions, executed via the bank treasury interface with next-day settlement; and (4) PSP aggregation for mass low-value payouts (e.g., affiliate, bug-bounty, or beta-testing networks) routed through Wise or Airwallex or the bank's virtual-account module, avoiding fractional SWIFT fees. Apple IAP and Google Play Billing net settlements arrive by electronic transfer from Apple Distribution International (Ireland) or Google Asia Pacific (Singapore), as applicable, and are swept automatically to the Operational Account. If CAD conversion is sought, FX is priced under a two-way quote from the bank's treasury; otherwise the funds may be retained in USD under a USD sub-ledger. Non-resident partner distributions require a formal General Partner resolution, Part XIII withholding may be applied inside the wire (funds sent net of Canadian withholding tax), and the T5013 reporting will be completed by the tax preparer.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable vanilla FX forwards (CAD/USD, CAD/EUR, CAD/GBP, CAD/CNH) up to 24-month tenors under an ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with a Canadian credit-support annex; suitable for locking the CAD/USD conversion of quarterly Apple and Google proceeds or of capital-call draws.

Plain-vanilla European FX options (purchases only) providing asymmetric budget protection for anticipated capital expenditures (e.g., USD-denominated cloud procurement); resale of options is treated as speculative trading and is prohibited under the treasury policy.
Cross-currency swaps (XCCY/CCIRS) converting USD-denominated operational obligations into CAD-floating or CAD-fixed equivalents for multi-year supplier contracts, with each leg separately documented.

CME Group and Montreal Exchange (MX) CAD/USD and CAD/EUR futures, used only when the underlying exposure notional is equal or larger and executed exclusively through a registered derivatives dealer; transactions may be physically or cash-settled at the LP's election.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for genuinely non-convertible emerging-market settlement currencies (e.g., CNH, INR, IDR) where the app treasury faces content-localisation, advertising, or distribution costs; NDFs on CAD are not market-conventional because the CAD spot market is fully deliverable and unrestricted.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction / Registrar of Companies
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within the anniversary-based filing window under the Alberta Partnership Act; generally by the last day of the month following the registration-anniversary month each year.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file may cause the Registry to place a registration hold; continued default permits cancellation or administrative strike-off of the limited partnership after written notice from the Registrar, with reinstatement fees and restoration conditions.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T5013 Partnership Information Return and Partner Allocation Schedules
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 5 months after the partnership fiscal period-end; May 31 for calendar-year-end limited partnerships.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: CRA late-filing penalty of CAD 20 per day, minimum CAD 100 and maximum CAD 2,500, plus potential gross-negligence or repeated-failure penalties and partner-level compliance assessments.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No mandatory Alberta statutory audit solely because the entity is a limited partnership. A compulsory independent audit is triggered only if the LP is a reporting issuer under Canadian securities legislation, is registered in a regulated financial activity, or becomes subject to an audit requirement in a unanimous partner agreement or lender/funding covenant.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Non-reporting Canadian private partnership: CPA Canada Handbook - Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE); reporting issuer or explicitly elected partnership: IFRS. Financial records must be maintained on an accrual basis under the Income Tax Act for T5013 reporting.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta does not operate a separate public UBO registry for limited partnerships. The annual return must confirm the identity, address, contribution amount, and allocation percentage of each general and limited partner. Any transfer of partnership interests during the year must be documented in the transfer register; a change of general partner or registered office triggers a Registry amendment filing.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of General Partners and Limited Partners
Register of Partnership Interest Transfers and Assignments
Registered Office and Principal Place of Business Record
Minute Book containing unanimous partner agreements, consents, and meeting records

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 2,500–8,000 if required by partner agreement or lender; normally nil for a non-reporting Alberta limited partnership

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined general corporate income tax rate for Alberta corporations: 15% federal plus 8% Alberta. A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation may generally access an 11% combined small-business rate on eligible active business income up to the applicable CAD 500,000 business limit. A Canadian limited partnership is generally fiscally transparent and does not itself pay corporate income tax; income and losses are allocated to partners.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No general corporate tax holiday. Qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations may claim the federal small-business deduction and Alberta small-business rate. Eligible software development and technology expenditures may qualify for federal and Alberta scientific research and experimental development incentives, subject to statutory eligibility, documentation, and expenditure rules. Federal refundable SR&ED credits can be up to 35% for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations within the applicable expenditure limit and generally 15% otherwise; Alberta incentives must be separately tested. Partnership-level income is generally taxed in the hands of the partners, with tax attributes subject to partnership and partner-level restrictions.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: CRA Form T5013, Partnership Information Return, including applicable T5013 slips and summaries, filed electronically through CRA-approved T5013 Internet Filing software or an authorized representative using Represent a Client. The LP generally files the partnership information return; it does not file a T2 solely because it is an LP.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Generally due within five months after the end of the partnership fiscal period. For a December 31 year-end, the normal deadline is May 31 of the following year. T5013 slips and partner information must be provided within the same statutory filing cycle.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, business number, T5013 program account, partnership address, fiscal period, jurisdiction of residence, and partnership type.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the exact registered LP name and CRA business number. Identify non-resident partners and maintain Canadian permanent-establishment and treaty-residency analysis where relevant.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Principal business activity, applicable NAICS classification, business revenues, expenses, and income or loss.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report Canadian business activity and allocate income by partner under the partnership agreement and Canadian tax rules. Do not treat Apple or Google platform receipts as automatically foreign-source merely because settlement occurs outside Canada.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross revenue, cost of sales, advertising, cloud services, software development, professional fees, payment-platform fees, salaries, interest, depreciation, and other deductible expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply Canadian deductibility, capitalization, withholding, related-party, and foreign-exchange rules. Separate current expenses from depreciable property and eligible SR&ED expenditures.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Each partner's name, address, taxpayer identification number, partnership percentage, allocated income or loss, capital account information, and relevant tax attributes.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Obtain accurate foreign tax identification numbers and residency information. Allocate income consistently with the legal agreement, profit-sharing terms, and Canadian anti-avoidance rules; report non-resident partner amounts on the applicable T5013 slip.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Business income or loss, other income, interest, dividends, capital gains, foreign income, deductions, and relevant source-specific amounts.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Preserve source characterization because non-resident partners may have Canadian filing, withholding, treaty, and permanent-establishment consequences. Foreign income does not eliminate Canadian reporting where the partnership carries on business in Canada.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign property, foreign accrual property income, related-party transactions, and other information required by the T5013 package or related CRA forms.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Determine separately whether Form T106, T1135, T1134, or other information returns apply to the LP or its partners. Do not consolidate partner-level reporting obligations into the T5013 unless the applicable form expressly requires it.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: GST/HST registration, collected tax, input tax credits, and filing-period information where the LP is a registrant.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Test registration and place-of-supply rules for Canadian app users, digital supplies, platform intermediation, and non-resident platform operators. GST/HST compliance is separate from income-tax filing.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T5013 filing is generally subject to an administrative penalty calculated at CAD 25 per day, subject to statutory minimum and maximum amounts, with additional penalties for repeated or deliberate non-compliance and failure to provide required information. A corporate partner required to file Form T2 generally faces a late-filing penalty of 5% of unpaid balance plus 1% per complete month late, up to 12 months, with higher penalties for repeated failures. Interest accrues on unpaid tax and instalment deficiencies.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: CRA Form T2, Corporation Income Tax Return, filed electronically through CRA Corporation Internet Filing or approved tax software by a corporate partner or by any incorporated entity conducting the business. Alberta corporate income tax is administered through the federal T2 system.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; corporate tax instalments are generally monthly or quarterly where applicable
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: A corporation generally files within six months after its taxation year-end. Any balance is generally due two months after year-end, or three months for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations meeting statutory conditions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation of accounting income to taxable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Adjust for non-deductible expenses, reserves, depreciation, partnership allocations, foreign exchange, shareholder benefits, and Canadian tax limitations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculation and utilization of non-capital and net capital losses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply the Canadian loss carryback and carryforward rules, acquisition-of-control restrictions, stop-loss provisions, and partnership basis limitations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Associated corporations, ownership, and small-business-limit allocation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Identify foreign and Canadian associated corporations and test controlled-private-corporation status. A non-resident-owned corporation generally cannot claim the Canadian-controlled private corporation benefits.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 23 or applicable small-business schedules
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal small-business deduction and related calculations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use only where statutory Canadian-controlled private corporation conditions are satisfied. Partnership active-business income may require allocation and specified-partner analysis.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income earned in a province or territory and provincial allocation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate Alberta income using applicable Canadian provincial allocation rules and maintain payroll, revenue, and permanent-establishment support.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 Schedule 8 and capital cost allowance
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital cost allowance for depreciable property, including software and equipment.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Classify acquired software, development assets, servers, and equipment under the correct Canadian capital-cost-allowance rules; distinguish qualifying SR&ED expenditures.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal SR&ED expenditures and investment tax credit claims.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Maintain contemporaneous technical narratives, time records, project costs, subcontractor records, and ownership evidence. App-store commercialization alone does not establish SR&ED eligibility.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information return for non-arm's-length transactions with non-residents.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File where the statutory reporting conditions are met, including applicable transaction-value thresholds. Reconcile T106 data with transfer-pricing documentation, general ledger records, and withholding returns.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late or deficient T2 filings can trigger percentage-based late-filing penalties, instalment interest, arrears interest, repeated-failure penalties, gross-negligence penalties, and prosecution for deliberate non-compliance. T106 failures can trigger penalties calculated by period of non-compliance, with additional penalties where documentation or information is deliberately withheld.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: CRA Forms NR4 and applicable Part XIII withholding remittances, generally administered through CRA My Business Account, Represent a Client, and CRA electronic remittance channels.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Monthly withholding remittance; annual NR4 information return
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Amounts withheld under Part XIII are generally remitted by the 15th day of the month following the month of payment or credit. NR4 slips and the annual summary are generally due by the last day of March following the calendar year.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross income paid or credited to the non-resident.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report the actual Canadian-source royalty, interest, dividend, or other Part XIII amount before withholding.
Apply the domestic rate unless a valid treaty-reduction process has been completed and beneficial ownership, residence, entitlement, and limitation-on-benefits conditions are supported.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, address, country code, and foreign taxpayer identification information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the beneficial owner's identity, not merely an intermediary or payment processor, unless the intermediary is legally the recipient and beneficial-ownership analysis supports that treatment.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late remittances generally attract penalties of 10% of the amount required to be remitted, or 20% for a second or later failure in the relevant period, plus arrears interest. Failure to file NR4 information returns, incorrect slips, or failure to withhold can create additional penalties, director exposure, and personal liability for responsible officers in appropriate cases.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII withholding on taxable dividends paid or credited to a non-resident, subject to an applicable tax treaty. Common treaty outcomes include 5% for a qualifying corporate shareholder meeting ownership and limitation-on-benefits conditions and 15% for other qualifying dividends. The exact rate depends on the recipient's residence, beneficial ownership, ownership percentage, treaty article, and anti-treaty-shopping rules.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: Obtain a valid certificate of residence or equivalent reliable evidence from the beneficial owner before applying a reduced rate. Collect ownership, beneficial-ownership, entitlement, limitation-on-benefits, and treaty-residence support; complete any payer due-diligence procedures; retain documentation for CRA review; and remit and report the reduced amount on the NR4 only where legally supportable. A Canadian payer normally does not obtain advance CRA approval for ordinary treaty relief, but CRA may reassess the payer for under-withholding.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Domestic Part XIII rate is generally 25% on Canadian-source royalties and interest paid or credited to non-residents. Treaty royalty rates commonly range from 0% to 15%, and treaty interest rates commonly range from 0% to 15%, depending on the treaty and payment type. Arm's-length interest is generally exempt from Canadian withholding under domestic rules, subject to statutory exceptions, including certain participating debt interest and non-arm's-length situations. Software, copyright, trademark, know-how, cloud, platform, and technical-service payments require separate characterization; treaty business-profit provisions may apply where the amount is not a royalty and the recipient lacks a Canadian permanent establishment.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 aggregate value of non-arm's-length cross-border transactions is the principal statutory threshold commonly relevant to contemporaneous documentation requirements and Form T106 reporting, subject to the precise transaction categories and exceptions. For multinational enterprise groups, the Canadian country-by-country reporting threshold is generally EUR 750,000,000 of consolidated group revenue, converted under the applicable rules. Canadian rules do not use a universal OECD-style Local File threshold for every transaction; documentation must be sufficient to support arm's-length pricing whenever section 247 applies.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada has no standalone general Economic Substance Regulation regime equivalent to certain offshore ESR statutes. Substance is nevertheless relevant under the Income Tax Act, including the general anti-avoidance rule, sham doctrine, beneficial-ownership principles, transfer-pricing rules, thin-capitalization rules, foreign-affiliate and FAPI rules, treaty anti-abuse provisions, and principal-purpose or limitation-on-benefits provisions. An LP claiming treaty or Canadian tax outcomes should maintain genuine business activity, personnel or outsourced operational capacity, decision-making records, contractual control, risk assumption, IP functions, and commercially coherent cash flows.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Concealing app revenue, falsifying development expenses, claiming personal costs as business deductions, omitting partnership income, or submitting materially false T5013, T2, T106, GST/HST, or withholding information.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Assessment of unpaid tax, arrears interest, gross-negligence penalty generally equal to the greater of CAD 100 and 50% of the understated tax or overstated credit, civil fraud penalties, and criminal prosecution. Tax evasion convictions can result in fines of 50% to 200% of the tax evaded and imprisonment of up to five years under the Income Tax Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and responsible officers may face prosecution, fines, imprisonment, and director-liability assessments for unremitted source deductions where statutory conditions are met. Corporate separateness is not a shield for personal participation in fraud. Travel restrictions are not an automatic tax penalty but may arise through criminal-process orders, bail conditions, or enforcement proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Withhold or Remit Non-Resident Tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, royalties, or taxable interest to non-residents without applying the correct Part XIII rate, relying on an invalid treaty certificate, or failing to remit withheld amounts.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Payer assessment for the unwithheld amount, applicable late-remittance penalties, interest, failure-to-file penalties, and potential director liability for source deductions and remittances.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be jointly and severally liable for corporate source deductions and withholding amounts where the statutory due-diligence defense is unavailable. Criminal liability may arise for deliberate obstruction, falsification, or fraud.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging non-arm's-length royalties, management fees, cloud-service fees, development fees, or financing returns that are unsupported by functions, assets, risks, comparable evidence, or actual commercial benefit.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA may adjust Canadian income under Income Tax Act section 247, impose a transfer-pricing penalty generally equal to 10% of the amount of an adjustment not reasonably documented or reported, deny deductions, reassess withholding, and apply interest. Recharacterization may occur where the legal form does not reflect the commercial substance.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are not ordinarily personally liable merely because an adjustment is made, but personal exposure can arise from knowing participation in false records, fraud, obstruction, source-deduction failures, or criminal tax conduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using an LP to disguise employment, agency, or corporate operations; allocating losses without economic entitlement; exceeding limited-partner at-risk amounts; or arranging artificial loss transfers.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Denial or reallocation of partnership losses, application of at-risk and limited-partner rules, reassessment of partners, interest, penalties, and possible GAAR application. A partnership may also be recharacterized for specific tax purposes based on its legal and commercial facts.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: General partners may have broader contractual and statutory liability than limited partners. Limited partners may lose limited-liability protection if they participate in management contrary to applicable provincial law or if the structure is otherwise disregarded. Fraudulent conduct can create personal civil and criminal exposure.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Routing dividends, interest, or royalties through an entity with no meaningful personnel, functions, control, risk, or beneficial ownership, solely to obtain a lower Canadian treaty rate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Denial of treaty benefits under beneficial-ownership, limitation-on-benefits, principal-purpose, anti-conduit, or GAAR principles; reassessment of withholding; interest; penalties; and possible prosecution where records are knowingly false.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Individuals who knowingly establish or operate a conduit structure may face civil recovery, director-liability claims, penalties, and criminal prosecution. A travel ban is not automatic but may be imposed by a court in criminal proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Undeclared Foreign Affiliate, Foreign Asset, or Related-Party Reporting
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to report foreign affiliates, specified foreign property, related-party cross-border transactions, foreign accrual property income, or beneficial ownership interests.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Failure-to-file penalties, extended reassessment periods, denial of deductions or foreign tax relief, interest, gross-negligence penalties, and prosecution for deliberate concealment. Applicable filings may include T106, T1134, T1135, and country-by-country reports.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Personal liability generally depends on the specific tax, withholding, payroll, or criminal provision. Knowing falsification or obstruction may expose directors and officers to fines and imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to register, collect, report, or remit GST/HST on taxable digital supplies, or incorrectly treating app-store settlements and platform commissions as outside the Canadian place-of-supply rules.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Assessment of uncollected GST/HST, interest, late-filing and late-remittance penalties, denial of unsupported input tax credits, and possible prosecution for fraud or deliberate evasion.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be liable for unremitted GST/HST in accordance with statutory director-liability provisions, subject to available due-diligence defenses. Deliberate evasion can result in criminal fines and imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML, Proceeds of Crime, and Sanctions
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using app revenue, payment accounts, cryptoassets, or related-party transfers to launder proceeds, evade sanctions, conceal beneficial ownership, or circumvent Canadian financial-monitoring requirements.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Asset seizure and forfeiture, administrative monetary penalties, prosecution under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and Criminal Code, and sanctions-related criminal or administrative consequences.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors, officers, and beneficial owners may face personal fines, imprisonment, forfeiture, prohibition orders, and court-imposed travel or bail restrictions. Corporate liability does not prevent prosecution of individuals who authorized, directed, or knowingly facilitated the conduct.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Destroying accounting records, deleting transfer-pricing evidence, backdating agreements, misleading CRA officials, or obstructing an audit or examination.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Record-keeping penalties, adverse evidentiary inferences, extended reassessment periods, gross-negligence or fraud penalties, prosecution, fines, and imprisonment for obstruction or related criminal conduct.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Individuals who direct or participate in destruction, obstruction, or fabrication may be personally prosecuted and imprisoned. Civil veil-piercing is fact-specific and is not automatic solely because the corporation or LP is insolvent.
